references.text: The women returned from the tomb and told all these things to the eleven and to all the rest (Luke 24:9). Here we see the same group – 'the eleven' – that the Emmaus travelers now find gathered in Jerusalem.
The continuation of the story where the eleven confirm that the Lord has indeed risen and appeared to Simon (Luke 24:34-35), which connects directly with the return of the Emmaus travelers.
In Mark 16:13 it is briefly told that the two went and told this to the others, but they were not believed – a parallel to the Emmaus travelers' return to the group of disciples.
John tells us that the disciples were gathered behind locked doors that same evening (John 20:19). This is the same gathering that the Emmaus travelers found when they returned to Jerusalem.
After the ascension, the eleven were gathered in Jerusalem in prayer (Acts 1:13-14). The pattern of the disciples gathering in Jerusalem after important events recurs.

Paul confirms that Christ appeared to the twelve (1 Corinthians 15:5), a reference to the same group of disciples (here called 'the twelve' as a designation for the group, even though there were eleven).

Cleopas and his companion were on their way to Emmaus (Luke 24:18). Now they hurry back to Jerusalem – the expression 'rose up in that very hour' (αὐτῇ τῇ ὥρᾳ) shows that they left Emmaus immediately after recognizing Jesus.
The group is referred to as 'the eleven' because Judas had fallen away. Only after the choice of Matthias was the number again twelve (Acts 1:26).
Also in Matthew 28:16 the group is called 'the eleven disciples' who met the risen Jesus, which agrees with the designation used here in Luke.
